Copper Quarterly Report October 2008 

# Executive Summary 

## Copper Crumbles – the $64bn question 



- We have revised down our forecasts of both consumption and production from those presented before LME Week in our Executive Preview to reflect the impact of financial crisis on the real economy. 



- The refined copper market is expected to remain finely balanced although inventory levels will build through the final quarter of this year.  We expect to see substantial surpluses emerging from 2009, forcing prices sharply lower. 



- The financial crisis is already curtailing both consumption and production growth.  The race is now on between supply and demand – which will suffer the greater decline and what effect that will have on the overall supply/demand position. 



- History tells us that commodity booms usually end up with a demand side shock – in this regards, this boom is ending no differently.  In the immediate future the impact on demand will be greater.  Suppliers have already announced their intention to review their production plans and project pipelines in response to the financial crisis - a much quicker reaction than in previous cycles.  That said, we are still on a higher growth path due to China. 



- Uncertainty remains the dominant theme across all markets at present, even though global stock markets have recovered from their lows and interbank lending rates have crept down a little.  As the Federal Reserve chairman Ben Bernanke suggested, the bail-outs may not be over yet; and the US economy might need another “stimulus package” on top of the $150bn in rebates sent out to taxpayers earlier this year. 



- In the short term we remain of the view that sentiment rather than the fundamentals will be the main driving force of price movements.  The base metals markets have remained volatile, with all six LME metals recording double digit declines since the end of September.  Copper has not been immune.  Over the period to 21<sup>st</sup> October, the 3-month copper price has traded from a high of $6,510/t to lows of $4,440/t, a loss of 30% in just fifteen days of trading.

October 2008 Executive Summary Financing has now become a major concern for both consumers and producers. Projects will be affected across the entire supply chain with mines, smelters and refinery expansions at risk. Mid-tier and junior mining companies have the highest risk, with several mining projects already having been suspended. We expect projects scheduled beyond 2010 will be delayed by 12 months as credit constraints are put in place. Spot interest for refined copper has come to a halt. Fabricators are reluctant to conclude 2009 annual contracts too soon amid the uncertainty from their end-consumers as the contagion from the financial crisis spreads to the real economy. Consumers will destock and look to consume scrap (where possible) in place of refined metal. We anticipate a significant slowdown in the US, Europe and other developed regions while exports of copper products (and copper-containing products) from China and other developing regions are set to decline. We anticipate that domestic demand in these regions will remain robust benefiting from structurally-driven consumption growth. ### Copper prices succumb to financial meltdown ###### LME cash price and supply/demand balance, quarterly, 2002-2010 000t Cu

The actual numbers we have for the first half of the year - which was stronger - do suggest that sentiment is maybe worse than the facts and remain of the view that world refined demand growth will be 1.5% this year. The financial crisis and consequent economic slowdown will lead to further declines in copper demand in 2009. The crisis will impact nations in several ways. Some will be directly affected by the exposure of their banking system to toxic loans. But even countries whose banking sectors emerge relatively unscathed are likely to be hit by weakening exports, and by greater difficulty obtaining credit, which will stifle investment. Confidence is much lower; and the importance of negative sentiment as a transmission mechanism should not be underestimated. We have significantly revised down our forecast for growth in 2009 to 1.9%. We expect that the developed regions of North America, Europe and North East Asia will all see refined copper consumption fall next year. Demand in China and other developing countries will also suffer. We now anticipate that Chinese refined demand growth will be 5.5% in 2009. We assume that heavy infrastructure development boosted by government initiatives will enable China to maintain positive growth next year, while its export related portion, around 25-30% of total copper consumption, will decline slightly. 000t

Ongoing structural development in China and some of the other emerging countries, such as the Gulf States, will support world growth next year. Although we do not expect these countries to be unaffected by the crisis, infrastructure programmes, ultimately underwritten by reserves, and in some cases, such as China, backed up by fiscal surpluses, should support demand growth. China recently announced a series of measures which should maintain domestic growth. Developed nations too, are likely to attempt to stimulate domestic consumption through infrastructure projects. This is likely to be easiest for those countries such as Spain and Germany with large fiscal surpluses. The UK has recently announced intentions to bring CRU International Limi

forward the start dates of several major infrastructure projects.  Presidential candidate Barack Obama has suggested that he may implement a US$50B infrastructure programme if elected. 

Where this downturn differs from previous recessions is the limited inventory overhang through the consumption chain.  This means that there is relatively little scope to run down stocks and should also help speed up the recovery.  We expect copper consumers to live hand-to-mouth for some time and expect talks over long-term contracts to be pushed onto the back burner for the time being.  Consumers will be unwilling to commit to any long term contracts too soon given the unpredictable market environment.  Moreover, the fallout from the turmoil in the global markets will force consumers to re-consider their investment profile and how they should manage their risk exposure to counterparties. 

Substitution will remain a significant issue for the market, despite the recent declines in the copper price.  The downturn will increase pressure to switch to cheaper materials, less volatile commodities and away from copper.  There is a concerted effort by the US air conditioner industry to look at switching to aluminium rather than copper tube.  Aluminium also continues to pose a threat in the winding wire and heat exchanger markets. 

#### Project delays to add to production shortfalls 

Global production continues to disappoint and we are now approaching what appears to be the sixth consecutive year of shortages.  As we look ahead, we expect production to continue to under-perform, but with the outlook for refined demand so uncertain, disappointing supply side news has taken a back seat for now. 

Nevertheless, the tale of woe persists at mines with losses incurred as a result of strikes (kidd Creek), equipment failure (Lumwana) and infrastructure strain (Escondida and Collahuasi). Milling rates creep higher while head grades decline (at at Grasberg, Escondida and Alumbrera) as mines are operated at capacity.  Copper has continued to suffer from industrial action this year, particularly in Chile and Mexico, with sporadic activity in Peru and to a lesser extent Zambia.  The power shortages which were a feature of the market earlier this year have abated, although power infrastructure remains strained across south and central Africa, both as a result of increased mining activity and copper power cable thefts.  Water issues associated with both supply infrastructure and environmental regulations are also becoming increasingly significant across key mining regions such as Chile and the African Copper belt. 

Three major projects (Safford, Gabriela Mistral and Luita) have however been commissioned in 2008, all of which are EW cathode producers.  The lack of any new concentrates projects (Prominent Hill is not yet operating) combined with problems at Escondida, Collahuasi, Alumbrera, Grasberg and

Batu Hijau this year mean that concentrates production has been particularly muted. CRU now forecasts a 1% reduction in concentrate production this year, before recovering sharply in 2009 and 2010. We also expect a 2.5% increase in refined production to 18.5Mt this year, underpinned by strong growth in Chinese output, which will offset declines in a number of countries but particularly India, Chile and Mexico. Smelter output, however, is set to register a 0.9% decrease to 13.1Mt, due largely to lengthy maintenance closures in the first half of the year. Concentrates continue to be in tight supply limiting smelter output. The increase in refined output will be supported by higher EW output and growth in high grade scrap usage. New factors such as governance and regulation, and financial effects either as debt/credit problems, portfolio sequencing or strategic portfolio reductions are becoming increasingly significant. Expansions are increasingly reliant on brownfield projects as greenfield developments are delayed, over-budget and generally small. The credit crunch is likely to push the development of a fair number of projects back to beyond 2010. A large increase in new capacity is still, however, forecast for 2010 and beyond. Financial restrictions as a result of the “credit crunch” will have an impact on the speed of project development and we have made a global adjustment to production to take account of this. It is impossible to assess the impact of the “credit crunch” on a case by case, so we have maintained our mine by mine production forecasts, including those for projects, and made a “bottom line” adjustment to total refined production to account for this. Any restrictions on mine output are assumed to feed directly through to refined copper output. Given the tightness of the concentrates market any mine cutbacks will have a direct impact on smelter and refined production, while reductions at SXEW mines will obviously impact cathode production. Known plans call for a significant increase in global refined copper output, with committed output forecast to increase to 22.2M tonnes by 2013. However we do not expect this figure to be achieved, primarily because there will be insufficient raw materials available. Even before the financial crisis hit, mine supply was expected to fall short of smelters’ concentrate requirements by up to a million tonnes contained copper. Financial restrictions are now expected to result in additional project development delays, further limiting the availability of concentrates for smelting. In addition, smelting and refinery projects will also be affected by financial restrictions, while weak refined copper demand will discourage investment in new capacity. There may also be delays to new SXEW projects, while the forecast decline in prices may lead to the temporary suspension of high cost mines. ### China will account for most of

CRU International Limited confidential 8 Copper Quarterly Report October 2008 Executive Summary #### Copper concentrates stocks at minimum working levels The concentrates market has showed a statistical deficit during the first three quarters of the year, with the draw down in stocks estimated to have totalled around 140,000t contained copper. The deficit has, however shrunk during the year as mine production has increased while maintenance closures and technical problems have reduced smelter demand. Worldwide stocks are now extremely low, with most smelters working with minimum levels. There has been an increase in the number of swap deals carried out and the gravity of the situation was highlighted recently when a delayed shipment left a Far East smelter with just days’ of inventory. A time swap was arranged allowing material that was already on the water to be delivered. The recent force majeure announcement by BHP Billiton on deliveries of concentrates from its Escondida mine has exacerbated the shortfall problem. As the chart below shows, our forecasts of mine and smelter production indicate that mine production will continue to fall short of smelters’ potential consumption over the forecast period. At current stock levels these shortfalls cannot occur without further smelter cutbacks. 9 

The current turmoil in the financial markets and the downturn in the world economy will affect both the mining and smelting industries, as they react to restrictions on the availability of credit, declining copper prices and the contraction in demand for refined copper. 

We also expect smelters to suffer in the forthcoming TC/RC annual negotiations as their byproduct lifeline fails.  Falling sulphuric acid credits, a reduction in the value of free metal, lower precious metals prices and another drop in the value of brick contracts will combine to push many smelters into the red during 2009. 

Further in to the forecast period we expect delays to mining and smelting projects.  Our Beijing office has already reported on delays to new capacity development in China due to financial restrictions and shortages of raw materials.  We anticipate that there will be further project delays.  These delays will be apparent in the primary smelter feed balance from as earlier as 2010. 

#### Points to watch 

As this financial crisis unfolds, we anticipate a downturn in consumption and a sharp decline in prices.  History tells us that prices in a recession can fall well below the level where high cost producers fail to cover their costs.  By our calculations, and compared to our forecasts presented in the July Copper Quarterly and those presented here, we estimate that the producers will see a loss of revenue to the tune of $64Bn.  How will industry adjust? 

Cutbacks on shareholder returns/dividends 



Investment reassessment 



- Project pipelines 



- Exploration 



- Labour 



Short term avoidable o capital expenditure and maintenance 

We have also considered the likely impact of an alternative scenario – the collapse of demand and a sharp fall in the price as stocks mount, which is discussed in more detail in the Chapters. 

**_Supply_** : The persistent mine underperformance over the last few years will now be exacerbated by the lack of credit/finance as a result of the financial crisis.  How much will this reduce supply relative to demand?  We would expect to see cutbacks in production as high cost mines react to falling prices and additional project delays curtail refined copper output further. 

**_Demand_** : Will Chinese domestic copper consumption for infrastructure and construction as well as consumer durables offset the effect of the credit crunch and the reduction in exports of copper and copper-containing products? 

**_Stocks_** : Will the fall in prices lead to strategic stock building in Asia?  There have already been reports that the SRB might come back into the market to replenish inventories, particularly as prices tumble lower.  This could occur sooner rather than later. 

**_Funds_** : Have we reached capitula

tion or is there more unwinding of long positions to come? **_Economisation and substitution_** : Will the price falls lead to a narrowing of the gap between copper prices and those of competing materials (especially aluminium) and reduce the substitution threat?
